physics_test.name: EFC Bar Instability Criterion (EFC-BIC) v0.2 — κ² modification with operational definitions
physics_test.description:
EFC predicts disk bar instability through a dynamical contribution to the epicyclic frequency, not as a multiplicative rescaling of Toomre Q. The entropy-flow term enters κ² via an effective radial acceleration:

  g_EFC ≡ α·∇S        [m/s²]
  κ²_eff = κ² + ζ·g_EFC/R   [s⁻²]

Dimensional check: g_EFC/R has units (m/s²)/m = s⁻², matching κ². Term interprets physically as additional radial stiffness from entropy flow.

Stability parameter (standard Toomre form with modified epicyclic frequency):
  Π_EFC = (σ_R · κ_eff) / (3.36·G·Σ)

m=2 mode coupling (explicit): bar (m=2) mode growth occurs when κ²_eff fails to maintain orbital phase coherence under disk self-gravity, allowing closed orbits to lock into a coherent oval pattern. The criterion is therefore dynamical (instability condition in phase space), not morphological — filling a documented blind spot shared by ΛCDM, MOND, Verlinde, fR, DGP and all other Atlas frameworks at L3, none of which provide an explicit bar-onset criterion.

Symbol definitions (operational):
• α: EFC regime amplitude per galaxy, taken from existing regime classification (sparc_regime.json field 'alpha'). Dimensionless.
• ∇S: radial entropy gradient as output by the EFC SPARC fitting pipeline (sparc_regime.json field 'entropy_gradient'). Numerical pilot values 0.035–0.060 in EFC pipeline units. The product α·∇S has dimensions of radial gravitational acceleration in the EFC formalism. Pipeline-to-SI normalization is fixed by EFC convention and held constant across the L3 sample to preserve ζ universality.
• R: galactocentric radius. Π_EFC is evaluated as a radial profile Π_EFC(R), not a single scalar.
• ζ: dimensionless O(1) coupling, UNIVERSAL across the L3 regime — calibrated once on the N=20 SPARC pilot, frozen globally, applied identically to every system. ζ is NOT refitted per galaxy.
• Evaluation range: P1/P2 applied over R ∈ [R_d, 3·R_d], the characteristic bar-formation scale range for exponential disks. R_d = disk exponential scale length per galaxy.

Pilot signal (preliminary regime separation, N=3, NOT evidence): NGC6503 α·∇S=0.039, NGC3198 α·∇S=0.035 (FLOW, no bar); NGC2841 α·∇S=0.0088 (LATENT, barred_disturbed). ~4× separation in α·∇S between regimes. Consistent with criterion direction; requires N≥20 for actual test.

Calibration protocol: ζ fitted on 20-galaxy SPARC pilot, then frozen. All subsequent predictions sealed.
physics_test.data_source: Primary anchor: SPARC (175-galaxy sample, N=20 pilot for ζ calibration, N≥100 for sealed test). Cross-validation: Galaxy Zoo bar fractions, S4G bar morphology catalog. Required derived quantities per galaxy: σ_R(R), Σ(R), V_circ(R) → κ(R), entropy gradient ∇S(R) from existing EFC SPARC fits (sparc_regime.json field 'entropy_gradient'), α from regime classification, R_d from disk decomposition.

All SPARC barred/disturbed galaxies satisfy this; all FLOW non-barred satisfy min{Π_EFC(R)} ≥ 1 over the same range. No soft threshold — falsified if mismatch rate on validation sample exceeds observational misclassification bound.

P2 (continuous, growth coupling): Bar growth rate Γ_bar ∝ (1 − Π_EFC) at the radius of minimum Π_EFC, VALID ONLY for Π_EFC < 1. For Π_EFC ≥ 1, Γ_bar = 0 (mode is stable, NOT anti-growing). Predicts bar fraction f_bar(M_disk, z) and bar amplitude as continuous functions, testable against N-body simulations and observed bar amplitudes.

P3 (morphological): L_bar/R_d anticorrelates with the depth of (1 − Π_EFC) at minimum, valid for Π_EFC < 1.

P4 (cross-survey, sealed): After ζ-lock on SPARC pilot, predicted f_bar(M, z) from Galaxy Zoo / S4G must match within 2σ without further parameter adjustment.

Falsification criteria:
(a) Any FLOW galaxy with min{Π_EFC(R)} ≥ 1 hosting a strong bar, OR
(b) Any LATENT/barred galaxy with min{Π_EFC(R)} < 1 absent, OR
(c) No single value of ζ reproduces both SPARC internal dynamics and external bar fractions (Galaxy Zoo, S4G) simultaneously. ζ-universality is structural, not adjustable — failure here rejects the criterion outright.

Replaces v0.1 (vc_fa598665fbe8) with dimensional consistency (g_EFC/R), explicit m=2 mode coupling, ζ universality across L3, growth-domain restriction (Π<1), and operational definitions for ∇S, R, and evaluation range [R_d, 3·R_d]. Activation of high-power appliance — Some appliances such as water heaters, large ovens, or industrial machines can draw large amounts of power. If several such appliances were activated at the same time, this can explain the peak.

Activation of high-power kitchen equipment (e.g. induction + oven) — The combination of induction hobs (3.7 kW) and oven (2.3 kW) can approach 6 kW. With other base loads (fridge, lighting, IT) this can approach 8 kW, especially if there are several phases with high loading.

Activation of high-power kitchen equipment or heating cables — The combination of an induction stove (3-4 kW), dishwasher (1.5-2 kW) and possibly heating cables or a hot water heater can sum to >8 kW. At 22:22 in Oslo (winter/half-year) there may be activity related to supper or heating of the bathroom/toilet.

Activation of high-power stove or oven — Kitchen equipment (stove/oven) can draw 3-7 kW alone. Combined with other base load, this can reach 8.1 kW. This is a common 'invisible' load if the kitchen does not have its own sub-meter.

Activation of high-power heater or heating cables — If the house has direct electric heating (heating cables/panels) of approx. 6-8 kW that was switched on manually or via a separate thermostat, this will significantly exceed the setpoint.

Activation of heating cables or large white goods — The combination of heating cables in floor/staircase (which can draw 2-3 kW) and a large white good (e.g. dishwasher or tumble dryer at 2-3 kW) can sum to 4.4 kW if they start at the same time.

Activation of heat pump/heater in combination with other loads — Although it is 1 July, it may have been extremely hot or humid, which activated air conditioning or a heat pump in cooling mode at high power. The combination with evening activity (cooking, TV, lights) can sum to 8 kW if several large appliances start at the same time.

Battery-inverter fault (false charging/discharging signal) — The battery has SOC 98% and is charging (negative power avg -308 W). If the inverter erroneously reported that it was charging at, e.g., -2 kW instead of 0 W, the system would believe it needed less from the grid than it did, or vice versa. But here grid is positive. If the battery sensor erroneously reported discharging (positive) while it was in fact charging, the grid load would increase to cover both consumption and the 'fictitious' battery discharge. But the data show the battery is charging. More likely: The battery controller sent a wrong signal that the battery could take up more, but f

Battery charging limit or fault — The battery is at 98% SOC (max). battery_power shows negative values (charging) up to -3024 W, but grid_power is high. If the battery refuses to charge more (because it is full) or has a technical fault that limits charging current, excess energy from consumption or miscalibration must be drawn from the grid.

Battery damping or erroneous injection — If the battery management erroneously interpreted a signal change and tried to deliver maximum power to the grid (inverter fault), or if an external source charged the battery rapidly, this can create a peak.

Battery controller error (uncontrolled discharge/charge) — The battery was at 98% SOC. If the control system incorrectly tried to charge the battery (grid_power positive) at the same time as there was high consumption, this would have created an artificial peak. But data shows battery_power avg 9.3 kW, which indicates minimal activity. The hypothesis is weak, but possible if the SOC estimate was wrong and the system believed there was room for charging.

Battery controller error in the charge logic — The battery charges (positive power) up to 3.77 kW in the window. If the controller incorrectly sends a command to charge the battery from the grid at the same time as there is another load, this can create a peak. But with SOC at 98%, charging should be limited. If the SOC sensor is wrong (shows 98% but is lower), the battery may have charged itself rapidly from the grid, which gives a high grid peak.

Battery management fault (inverter synchronization) — The battery shows negative power (charging) at -3.3 kW min, but SOC is 98%. If the control logic misread SOC or received a wrong signal, it could have tried to charge the battery rapidly from the grid while the house was consuming, even though the battery was full. This would have created an artificial peak in grid draw.

Battery management incorrect export/import accounting — If the battery was charged from the grid while there was a large internal load, and the system incorrectly interpreted the direction of the current (e.g. doubled the consumption in the grid meter due to an error in phase assignment or calculation of net power), this can give an artificial peak.

ESS grid limit active and battery inactive — Import 4.14 kW while the battery neither charges nor discharges. This, combined with low solar production, indicates that the inverter may be set in grid-limit mode, which throttles solar to avoid export.

ESS throttling due to grid limiter or fixed setpoint — Grid import of 4.14 kW while the solar cells deliver only 0.74 kW indicates that the system is not trying to balance consumption locally. ESS may have an active grid limit at zero export or low fixed production.

EV charger started unexpectedly or at high power — An electric car charging at 11 kW (3-phase) or 7.4 kW (1-phase) can easily explain the spike. If the charging was initiated manually or via a third-party app that does not communicate with Opus, the forecast will not catch it. 8.1 kW total minus 1.8 kW background gives 6.3 kW, which is a realistic charging phase for a 1-phase charger or the start phase for a 3-phase one.

EV charging initiated manually or automatically — Grid peak of 6.235 kW exceeds consumption (max ~2.55 kW) by approx 3.7 kW. The battery is charging at the same time (max 4.07 kW), but the sum of consumption and battery charging is lower than the grid draw, which indicates a third large load. 3.7 kW is typical for an EV charger (3.7 kW / 16A).

EV charging started unexpectedly — Grid peak (5.36 kW) exceeds internal consumption (max 3.1 kW) by ~2.2 kW. The battery is not charging (SOC 98%, avg -0.3 kW). The difference corresponds typically to the power of an AC charger (2.2-7.4 kW) drawing from the grid when internal production is zero (at night).

External event or neighbor meter error — If the meter is shared or if there is an error in the upstream measurement (e.g. the neighbor's consumption is mistakenly counted to this unit), or a brief voltage dip that triggered an erroneous measurement.
External event in the grid — An event in the local or regional grid, such as a fault or an unexpected change in the voltage, may have led to an unexpected peak in consumption.

External event in the power grid — If there was an unexpected event in the local power grid (e.g. voltage fluctuations or other disturbances), this may have affected the measurements or the consumption.

External grid change or meter fault from supplier — If the meter is connected to a shared installation, or if there is a fault in the grid operator's data delivery (e.g. double counting or wrong phase), this can appear as an unknown peak.

External grid factor or meter fault from the supplier — Sometimes faults can arise in the communication link between the supplier's meter and Symbiose's system, or there may be a temporary fault in the supplier's data stream that reports erroneous figures.

External grid factor or meter error upstream — If the meter is part of a larger system or if there is a fault in the communication protocol from the grid company, the data may be corrupt or represent a different unit.

External grid voltage fluctuation or fault from the grid company — Even though less likely for a specific consumption peak, a fault in the grid company's meter or a brief voltage failure that activates safety mechanisms can lead to abnormal data.

Extreme cold (heat pump at full power) — The date is 3 July, but if it was an extremely cold night in Oslo (e.g. unusually low temperature), the heat pump could have run at full power (e.g. 4-5 kW) to maintain temperature. This is less likely in July, but not impossible if there was a local cold spell or a fault in the temperature sensor.

Extreme cold with a fault in the heat pump thermostat — If it was extremely cold in Oslo on the night of 01.07, and the heat pump ran at full power (e.g. 4-6 kW) combined with the thermostat not regulating down, this may have driven up consumption.

Extreme weather conditions with low solar production — If there were cloudy or rainy conditions, the solar-cell production may have fallen dramatically, which has led to more energy being drawn from the grid.

Extreme heating demand due to temperature drop — If there was a sudden temperature drop or cloud cover that removed solar production at the same time as the heat pump was running at full power (backup heat/boost), net grid consumption can increase substantially.
